quiz.say: His Letter to Marcellinus names a psalm for one need after another. Find the one he would give you.

name: Athanasius of Alexandria

seo.title: Athanasius of Alexandria: exiled five times, never silenced
seo.description: Athanasius of Alexandria in plain words: the deacon of Nicaea, his five exiles, the Life of Antony, the first list of our 27 books, and the myths.

band.lede: Four emperors drove him out of his city five times. He came home every time.

who: Athanasius was bishop of Alexandria, in Egypt, from 328 to 373. As a deacon he was at the Council of Nicaea. All his life he defended its faith: that the Son of God is truly God. Four emperors drove him out five times. He wrote the *Life of Antony*, and the first list of exactly our 27 New Testament books.

roles.name: Deacon

roles.name: Writer
roles.line: Of the *Life of Antony*, and a letter each Easter

roles.name: Peacemaker
roles.line: Called both sides to stop fighting over words, 362

lines: By four emperors, one after another

tidbits.text: Julian swore “by mighty Serapis” that if Athanasius was not out of Egypt by 1 December, he would fine the governor's own troops a hundred pounds of gold.

cite.text: Julian, Letter 46, to Ecdicius, prefect of Egypt, tr. W. C. Wright (1923)

tidbits.text: The day Julian died in Persia, Didymus, the blind teacher of Alexandria, saw riders in a vision. They said Julian had died that hour. Then: “send to Athanasius the bishop, that he too may know”.

cite.text: Palladius, Lausiac History, chapter 4, tr. W. K. Lowther Clarke (1918)

tidbits.text: At Trier, the city of his first exile, two officials of the emperor found a book in a monks' cottage “in which was written the life of Antony”. They read it and gave up their careers on the spot. Augustine heard the story in Milan, and it helped bring on his own conversion.

cite.text: Augustine, Confessions, Book 8, chapter 6

facts.label: Born
facts.text: About 296 to 298, most likely in Alexandria. The Greek synaxarion says his parents were Christians. The Coptic synaxarium says they were pagans, and that after his father died, Bishop Alexander baptized him and his mother.

facts.label: Bishop of
facts.text: **Alexandria**, in Egypt, from **8 June 328** until he died: 45 years. Older histories say 46, from an earlier date for his election.

facts.label: Died
facts.text: **2 May 373**, at home in Alexandria, aged about 75.

facts.label: Buried
facts.text: In Alexandria. Later accounts move his body to Constantinople, and then to Venice.

facts.label: Also called
facts.text: **Athanasius the Great**. **The Apostolic**, in the Coptic Church, which counts him its twentieth pope. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* calls him the “Father of Orthodoxy”.

facts.label: In looks
facts.text: Small. The emperor Julian sneered that he was “not even a man but only a contemptible puppet”. Gregory of Nazianzus found him “angelic in appearance, more angelic in mind”.

facts.label: Status
facts.text: A saint to Catholics, Orthodox, Copts, Anglicans and Lutherans. A **Doctor of the Church** in the Roman calendar.

facts.label: In art
facts.text: An old bishop with a grey or white beard, holding a book. Eastern icons often pair him with **Cyril of Alexandria**, who shares his day on 18 January.

facts.label: Wrote
facts.text: *On the Incarnation*, the *Discourses against the Arians*, the *Life of Antony*, defences of his own conduct, and a letter each Easter to the churches of Egypt.

portrait.alt: A Byzantine fresco: Athanasius, bald, with a curling beard, bows his head low before a gold halo on a deep blue wall. He wears a white vestment with large red crosses and holds an open scroll written in Greek. His name is painted beside his halo.
portrait.credit: Saint Athanasius the Great, a fresco by the painters Michael and Eutychios, church of the Mother of God Peribleptos, Ohrid, North Macedonia. Public domain.
portrait.creator: Michael and Eutychios
portrait.caption: Bowing at the altar, in a fresco by Michael and Eutychios in the church of the Peribleptos at Ohrid, North Macedonia, around 1300. The Greek beside his halo names him Athanasius the Great. Public domain.

gallery.alt: A Byzantine miniature on gold: two bishops in brown and blue robes, each holding a jewelled book, stand under two green arches on columns, above a strip of green ground
gallery.credit: Athanasius and Cyril of Alexandria, in the Menologion of Basil II, about 1000. Vatican Library. Public domain.
gallery.caption: Athanasius and Cyril of Alexandria, who share 18 January, in the *Menologion of Basil II*, a painted book of the saints' days made for a Byzantine emperor about the year 1000. Public domain.

gallery.alt: A Russian icon: Athanasius stands full length in a patterned vestment, blessing with his right hand and holding a jewelled book in his left, before a town of red towers and onion domes, with Christ in a small medallion above his halo
gallery.credit: Saint Athanasius, Archbishop of Alexandria, a Russian icon of the mid-1600s. Private collection. Public domain.
gallery.caption: A Russian icon of the mid-1600s. The painter drew Alexandria behind him as a Russian town, with onion domes. Private collection. Public domain.

west.text: **Catholic** memorial of a bishop and Doctor of the Church, and his day in the **1916 Roman Martyrology**. Also the **Church of England**, the **Episcopal Church**, and Lutherans in the **Missouri Synod** and the **ELCA**.

east.text: The **Greek** churches and the **OCA**, together with Cyril of Alexandria. The **Russian Church**, on the old calendar, keeps it on 31 January.
The **OCA**, and the **Russian Church** on the old calendar (15 May). The **Greek** calendar keeps it as the day his relics were moved.
The **Coptic** Church, on 7 Pashons in its own calendar: the day he died.

feasts.note: Why two days in the East? His own church's records put his death on 2 May, and the West keeps that day. The Greek synaxarion keeps his life on 18 January, and 2 May for the moving of his relics, of which, it says, no details are known. An editor of Gregory of Nazianzus in 1894 gives the older view: 18 January as “the day of the actual death”, and 2 May for the moving of his body to Hagia Sophia in Constantinople. Churches on the old calendar keep each date 13 days later.

traits.title: fierce on paper
traits.text: He could write savagely. Of the emperor Constantius he asked, “Now what is yet wanting to make him Antichrist?” The Meletians, a rival church in Egypt, were “like dogs unable to forget their vomit”. His own admiring editor, Archibald Robertson, called that book on Constantius “the one work which we would gladly believe to have come from any other pen”. Yet when Arius died, Athanasius wrote, “we ought not to insult the dead, though he be an enemy”.

cite.text: History of the Arians, chapter 76; Apology against the Arians, chapter 59; To the Bishops of Egypt, chapter 19; Robertson, Prolegomena (1892)

traits.title: gentle in person
traits.text: Gregory of Nazianzus called him “gentle, free from anger, sympathetic, sweet in words, sweeter in disposition”. When he came home from exile, Gregory says, “he treated so mildly and gently those who had injured him, that even they themselves, if I may say so, did not find his restoration distasteful”.

cite.text: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 21, chapters 9 and 30

traits.title: funny, even in danger
traits.text: Robertson wrote, “Like most men of great power, he had a real sense of humour.” Once, in Alexandria, a crow cawed, and some pagans asked him, mocking, what it said. He smiled. “It utters the sound cras,” he told them, and {la|cras} is Latin for “tomorrow”. Tomorrow, it meant, would not go well for them. The next day, says Sozomen, an order came from the emperor forbidding their festival.

cite.text: Sozomen, Church History, Book 4, chapter 10; Robertson, Prolegomena (1892)

traits.title: humble before God
traits.text: He fought all his life over who Christ is. Yet he wrote to monks who asked him about it: “For the more I desired to write, and endeavoured to force myself to understand the Divinity of the Word, so much the more did the knowledge thereof withdraw itself from me.”

cite.text: First Letter to Monks (Letter 52), chapter 1

traits.title: a peacemaker over words
traits.text: Christians who meant the same thing were quarrelling over the words for it. At his council of 362 he asked them “not to enquire further into each other's opinions, nor to fight about words to no useful purpose”. Gregory saw the result: “by permitting each party to use its own terms, he bound them together in unity of action”.

cite.text: Tome to the People of Antioch, chapter 8; Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 21, chapter 35

traits.title: immovable on the faith
traits.text: Gregory put it in one line: “to those who assailed him he was adamant, and to those at variance a magnet”. When Constantine ordered him to take Arius back, he refused. Robertson: “With Arius and Arianism no compromise was to be thought of.”

cite.text: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 21, chapter 31; Apology against the Arians, chapters 59 and 60; Robertson, Prolegomena (1892)

traits.title: not in it for himself
traits.text: His editor Robertson: “In the whole of our minute knowledge of his life there is a total lack of self-interest.” He treated Serapion and the monks “as equals or superiors, begging them to correct and alter anything amiss in his writings”.

cite.text: Robertson, Prolegomena to the Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, volume 4 (1892)

said.lede: Friends, emperors and a sceptic, in their own words.

quotes.q: In praising Athanasius, I shall be praising virtue.
quotes.who: Gregory of Nazianzus, preaching on his feast in Constantinople, about 380

cite.text: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 21, chapter 1

quotes.q: The worse the diseases of the Churches grow, the more do we all turn to your excellency, in the belief that your championship is the one consolation left to us in our troubles.
quotes.who: Basil of Caesarea, writing to him in his last years, and hoping one day to see him

cite.text: Basil, Letter 80

quotes.q: …Athanasius, the interpreter of the adorable Law, was sent away into Gaul for a time…
quotes.who: The young Constantine II, then Caesar, sending him home from Trier in 337

cite.text: Apology against the Arians, chapter 87

quotes.q: Infamous man! He has had the audacity to baptise Greek women of rank during my reign! Let him be driven forth!
quotes.who: The emperor Julian, in his own hand, at the foot of an order to the prefect of Egypt, 362

cite.text: Julian, Letter 46, tr. W. C. Wright (1923)

quotes.q: …Athanasius displayed a superiority of character and abilities, which would have qualified him, far better than the degenerate sons of Constantine, for the government of a great monarchy.
quotes.who: Edward Gibbon, the sceptical historian of Rome's fall, 1781

cite.text: Gibbon, The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire, chapter 21

moments.title: Bishop in a game
moments.text: Rufinus told this story first, and Socrates and Sozomen retold it. On the feast of Peter, a martyred bishop, Bishop Alexander looked out toward the sea. Children on the shore were playing church. Athanasius was their bishop, and he had baptized some who were not yet Christians. Alexander questioned them. They had done everything exactly as the Church does, so he let the baptisms stand. Then he had Athanasius brought up for the Church. Socrates thought it “not improbable”. His Victorian editor, Archibald Robertson, thought it “highly improbable”.

cite.text: Socrates, Church History, Book 1, chapter 15; Sozomen, Church History, Book 2, chapter 17; Robertson, Prolegomena (1892)

moments.title: The deacon at the council
moments.text: Alexander made him a deacon and his secretary. In 325 he took him to the great council at Nicaea. Arius, a priest of Alexandria, was teaching that the Son of God was created, and had a beginning. The council condemned him. Its creed said the Son is of one essence with the Father: in Greek, {el|ὁμοούσιος}. How much the young deacon did there is hard to say. Robertson thinks the winning side owed much “to the energy and eloquence of the deacon Athanasius”. Gregory of Nazianzus says that though he was “not yet ranked among the Bishops, he held the first rank among the members of the Council”.

cite.text: Sozomen, Church History, Book 2, chapter 17; Robertson, Prolegomena (1892); Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 21, chapter 14

moments.title: Chosen bishop
moments.text: Alexander died in the spring of 328. The bishops of Egypt later wrote that the whole church crowded together for days and nights, and “cried, shouted, that Athanasius should be Bishop”. They called him “good, pious, Christian, an ascetic, a genuine Bishop”. His enemies told another story: that six or seven bishops made him bishop “clandestinely in a secret place”. Sozomen, quoting Apolinarius, gives a third: Athanasius ran away to escape the honour, and the dying Alexander called out, “O Athanasius, thou thinkest to escape, but thou wilt not escape.” He was about thirty.

cite.text: Apology against the Arians, chapter 6; Sozomen, Church History, Book 2, chapter 17

moments.title: No to the emperor
moments.text: Eusebius of Nicomedia pressed him to take Arius back. Athanasius refused to receive men the council had condemned. Then a letter came from Constantine himself: “if I learn that you have hindered or excluded any who claim to be admitted into communion with the Church, I will immediately send some one who shall depose you by my command”. Athanasius wrote back that “that anti-Christian heresy had no communion with the Catholic Church”. He held his ground.

cite.text: Apology against the Arians, chapters 59 and 60

moments.title: The man with two hands
moments.text: His enemies said he had murdered Arsenius, a Meletian bishop, and cut off his hand for magic. They carried a hand about as proof. At the council of Tyre, Athanasius asked who there knew Arsenius. Several said they did. Then he brought in a man wrapped in a cloak, and turned back the cloak on one side to show one hand. He let them wait. Then he showed the other. “Arsenius, as you see, is found to have two hands: let my accusers show the place whence the third was cut off.” The council deposed him anyway.

cite.text: Socrates, Church History, Book 1, chapters 27 to 29; Sozomen, Church History, Book 2, chapter 25; Apology against the Arians, chapters 63 to 72

moments.title: The grain ships
moments.text: He went to the emperor himself. His enemies met him with a new charge: that he had threatened to stop the grain ships that fed the new capital. In his own words, they said “that Athanasius had threatened that he would cause the corn to be withheld which was sent from Alexandria to his own home”. Constantine, he says, “instead of granting me a hearing, he sent me away into Gaul”. He lived at Trier, on the Moselle, until Constantine died. He was home on 23 November 337.

cite.text: Apology against the Arians, chapter 87; Robertson, Prolegomena (1892)

moments.title: Antony comes to town
moments.text: The Arians claimed that Antony, the famous monk, agreed with them. So the old man came down from his mountain to Alexandria and taught the crowds that the Son of God is not a created being. Pagans came to the church asking to see “the man of God”. As many became Christians in those few days, Athanasius wrote, “as one would have seen made in a year”. When Antony left, Athanasius and others walked him to the city gate.

cite.text: Life of Antony, chapters 69 to 71

moments.title: Seven years away
moments.text: In 339 a council at Antioch named Gregory of Cappadocia bishop of Alexandria, and Gregory arrived that March. Athanasius left for Rome. Julius, bishop of Rome, and his council received him, and the Western bishops at Sardica cleared him in 343. By the reckoning of his own church, he was away seven years, six months and three days. He came home on 21 October 346, to what Robertson calls “the golden decade”.

cite.text: Robertson, Prolegomena (1892), from the Historia Acephala; Socrates, Church History, Book 2, chapter 22

moments.title: A psalm in the dark
moments.text: His people were keeping an all-night vigil in the church of Theonas. The general Syrianus surrounded it “with more than five thousand soldiers”. Athanasius sat down on his bishop's chair. He had a deacon read a psalm, with the people answering, “For His mercy endureth for ever”. It was Psalm 136. The soldiers broke in. His clergy begged him to go, and he refused until the people were out, “saying that it was better that my safety should be endangered, than that any of them should receive hurt”. At last monks dragged him away, and he slipped past the soldiers unseen.

cite.text: Defence of his Flight, chapter 24

moments.title: Six years hidden
moments.text: No one could find him. Robertson says he spent most of these years in the monks' cells of Upper and Lower Egypt, and part of them hidden in Alexandria itself. He probably wrote the *Life of Antony* now. Palladius, who met the woman herself when she was about seventy, says he hid all six years in her house in Alexandria. She was young then, and very beautiful, so no one would suspect her. She brought him books, “washing his feet herself”. Palladius's translator, W. K. Lowther Clarke, doubted it: “Athanasius may have hid for a little while in a virgin's house, but the story as it stands is unhistorical.” Meanwhile, in 359, the bishops of the West at Ariminum signed a creed that dropped Nicaea's word. Jerome looked back: “The whole world groaned, and was astonished to find itself Arian.”

cite.text: Robertson, Prolegomena (1892); Palladius, Lausiac History, chapter 63, tr. Lowther Clarke (1918); Jerome, Dialogue against the Luciferians, chapter 19

moments.title: Home on a colt
moments.text: Constantius died. His bishop at Alexandria, George, was lynched by the city's pagans, “in a way I cannot praise”, says Gregory of Nazianzus. The new emperor, Julian, let the exiled bishops go home. People came from all over Egypt to see Athanasius return. Gregory describes a homecoming like Palm Sunday, with branches, cloaks in the road, and a crowd like the Nile: “He rode upon a colt, almost, blame me not for folly, as my Jesus did upon that other colt.”

cite.text: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 21, chapters 26 to 29; Socrates, Church History, Book 3, chapters 2 to 4; Robertson, Prolegomena (1892)

moments.title: “Not far”
moments.text: Julian had let the exiles go home, not back to their churches, and Athanasius was baptizing pagans. Julian ordered him out. Athanasius told his friends, “Let us retire for a little while, friends; it is but a small cloud which will soon pass away.” He took a boat up the Nile. When he heard that Julian's officer was close behind, he had the boat turned round, and rowed back to meet him. In Theodoret's telling, the officer called out, “How far off is Athanasius?” “Not far,” said Athanasius, and the officer hurried on upriver. Julian was dead within the year.

cite.text: Socrates, Church History, Book 3, chapter 14; Theodoret, Church History, Book 3, chapter 5

moments.title: The last flight
moments.text: Under the Arian emperor Valens, an order came to expel him again. Soldiers broke into his church at night to take him. He had already gone. Socrates says he hid “for four entire months in an ancestral tomb”. Robertson, following an older chronicle, says he went to “a country house which belonged to him near the New River”. The city was near riot, and Valens gave way. On 1 February 366 he was restored for good.

cite.text: Socrates, Church History, Book 4, chapter 13; Robertson, Prolegomena (1892)

moments.title: The 27 books
moments.text: Every year he sent Egypt a letter to announce the date of Easter. In 367 he used it to list the books of the Bible, because people were reading others “called apocryphal”. His New Testament is exactly our 27 books, the first list known to match ours. His Old Testament has 22 books, one for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet. It includes Baruch, but not Esther. Esther he set with Wisdom, Sirach, Judith, Tobit, the *Didache* and the *Shepherd*: books not in the canon, but good for new believers to read. Of the canon he wrote: “Let no man add to these, neither let him take ought from these.”

cite.text: Festal Letter 39

extras.title: The charges against him
extras.lede: His enemies called him a sorcerer and a ruffian. His friends called every charge a lie. Some were plainly false. A letter found in Egypt shows that one was partly true.

items.title: The broken chalice
items.text: A man named Ischyras said that Macarius, a priest sent by Athanasius, had broken into his service, overturned the altar and smashed the cup. Athanasius's side said Ischyras was never a priest at all. The clergy of his district wrote that he “never had a Church”, and that only his own relations believed him. Ischyras once took the story back in writing, then told it again. Robertson notes how it grew: in one later council's letter, his cottage “becomes a basilica” that Athanasius had torn down.
items.quote: For he spread a report that he had suffered dreadfully in consequence of an assault; and that Macarius had rushed furiously toward the altar, had overturned the table, and broken a mystical cup.

cite.text: Socrates, Church History, Book 1, chapter 27; Apology against the Arians, chapter 74; Robertson, Prolegomena (1892)

items.title: The hand of Arsenius
items.text: The accusers had their own account of why they thought Arsenius was dead. A bishop under Athanasius, they said, had burned Arsenius's house, tied him to a pillar, whipped him and locked him up. Arsenius got out through a window and went into hiding, and when he did not reappear, “they naturally supposed him to be dead”. Athanasius's side said he had been paid to hide. After Tyre, Arsenius made his peace. He wrote to Athanasius as “dearly beloved Pope”, promising to keep the canons of the Church.
items.quote: …a bishop under the jurisdiction of Athanasius, named Plusian, had, at the command of his chief, burnt the house of Arsenius, fastened him to a column, and maltreated him with thongs, and then chained him in a cell.

cite.text: Sozomen, Church History, Book 2, chapter 25; Apology against the Arians, chapter 69; Robertson, Prolegomena (1892)

items.title: Violence against the Meletians
items.text: The Meletian bishops said at Tyre that he had beaten them and thrown them into prison. Most of what survives was written by his side. Then in 1924 H. Idris Bell of the British Museum published a letter from the other side, written by a Meletian named Callistus, most likely in 335. It says drunken soldiers beat Meletian monks, “and made them all bloody, so that they were in danger of death”. It says Athanasius himself had a bishop locked in the meat market. Bell judged that the charges “were in part true”. He thought it unlikely that Athanasius ordered the beatings, but doubted he did much to stop them. And he added that the letter too is one-sided, and that both parties were “tarred with the same brush”.
items.quote: We must conclude that there was a germ of truth in the picture given of Athanasius by his enemies as a self-willed, unruly man, apt to treat even the Imperial authority with contempt.

cite.text: Sozomen, Church History, Book 2, chapter 25; H. I. Bell, Jews and Christians in Egypt (1924), Papyrus 1914

extras.title: His letter on the Psalms
extras.lede: Our quiz *Which Psalm are you living right now?* is built on one of his letters. The lines here are our own translation from his Greek.

items.title: A friend who was ill
items.text: His friend Marcellinus was getting over an illness. He had spent the time reading the Psalms, trying to understand each one. Athanasius wrote back with what a studious old man had once taught him about them. He opens warmly:
items.quote: I admire your purpose in Christ, my friend Marcellinus.

cite.text: Letter to Marcellinus, chapter 1, our translation from the Greek (Migne, Patrologia Graeca 27)

items.title: A mirror
items.text: The rest of Scripture, the old man said, we read as other people's words. The Psalms we say as our own, as if they were written about us. He called them a mirror:
items.quote: And it seems to me that these words become a kind of mirror for the one who sings them, so that he sees himself in them, and the movements of his own soul; and so, having felt them, he speaks them out.

cite.text: Letter to Marcellinus, chapter 12, our translation from the Greek

items.title: A psalm for every need
items.text: Then the letter goes through one situation after another, and names the psalm to pray in each. Slandered? Psalm 52. Sinned? Psalm 51. Afraid? Psalm 118. Want to give thanks? Psalm 103. Our quiz uses 53 of his situations. You answer a few questions about your life now, and it gives you the psalm he named for it. He lived it, too. On the night the soldiers came in 356, the psalm he had read was Psalm 136.

cite.text: Letter to Marcellinus, chapters 15 to 28; Defence of his Flight, chapter 24

items.title: Bound in with the Bible
items.text: One of the oldest Bibles in the world, the Codex Alexandrinus of the 400s, is now in the British Library. In it, his letter comes right before the Book of Psalms.
items.quote: The Psalter, which contains the ψαλμὸς ἰδιόγραφος (cli.) and the liturgical canticles, is preceded by the Epistle of Athanasius to Marcellinus

cite.text: H. B. Swete, An Introduction to the Old Testament in Greek (1900)

words.note: His own words, in the English of the *Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers*, volume 4 (1892), edited by Archibald Robertson.

feature.q: For He was made man that we might be made God; and He manifested Himself by a body that we might receive the idea of the unseen Father; and He endured the insolence of men that we might inherit immortality.
feature.ctx: From *On the Incarnation*, which Robertson dated to about 318, when Athanasius was in his early twenties. The Greek verb he used means “made God”: {el|θεοποιηθῶμεν}.

cite.text: On the Incarnation, chapter 54

quotes.q: For the truth is not preached with swords or with darts, nor by means of soldiers; but by persuasion and counsel.
quotes.who: On an emperor who sent troops into church quarrels. Christ, he says, knocks at the door, and does not force it.

cite.text: History of the Arians, chapter 33

quotes.q: When did a judgment of the Church receive its validity from the Emperor?
quotes.who: On councils that deposed him at the emperor's word.

cite.text: History of the Arians, chapter 52

quotes.q: For although it be impossible to comprehend what God is, yet it is possible to say what He is not.
quotes.who: To monks who asked him to explain the faith.

cite.text: First Letter to Monks (Letter 52), chapter 2

quotes.q: But now that the Saviour has raised His body, death is no longer terrible; for all who believe in Christ tread him under as nought, and choose rather to die than to deny their faith in Christ.

cite.text: On the Incarnation, chapter 27

quotes.q: …while before your election you lived to yourself, after it, you live for your flock.
quotes.who: To Dracontius, a monk who ran away after being made a bishop.

cite.text: Letter to Dracontius (Letter 49), chapter 2

quotes.q: …for the crown is given not according to position, but according to action.
quotes.who: In the same letter, where he says there are “bishops who fast, and monks who eat”.

cite.text: Letter to Dracontius (Letter 49), chapter 9

quotes.q: For what else is the feast, but the service of the soul? And what is that service, but prolonged prayer to God, and unceasing thanksgiving?

cite.text: Festal Letter 3, chapter 2

myths.truth: It carries his name, but it is not his. Until the 1600s it was thought to be. In 1644 Gerard Voss pointed out that “no early writer of authority speaks of it as the work of this doctor”, and that its language looks Western, not Alexandrian. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* agrees it “most probably” cannot be his. The Lutheran Church–Missouri Synod says the creed, “though not composed by Athanasius, is named in his honor”.

cite.text: Catholic Encyclopedia (1907), “Athanasian Creed”; Lutheran Church–Missouri Synod, commemoration for 2 May

myths.claim: “If the world is against the truth, then I am against the world.”
myths.truth: Quote sites give this as his. We could not find it in his writings. Nor did we find the famous Latin tag {la|Athanasius contra mundum}, Athanasius against the world, in any ancient writer. The oldest form of the idea we found is Richard Hooker's, in 1597: “the whole world against Athanasius, and Athanasius against it”. In his own day, the man who stood alone was Liberius, bishop of Rome, speaking up for him. The emperor Constantius asked him, “What portion do you constitute of the universe, that you alone by yourself take part with an impious man?” Liberius answered, “My standing alone does not make the truth a whit the weaker.”

cite.text: Goodreads; Hooker, Laws of Ecclesiastical Polity, Book 5, chapter 42; Theodoret, Church History, Book 2, chapter 13

myths.claim: He spent twenty years in exile.
myths.truth: Gibbon wrote that “twenty years he passed as an exile or a fugitive”, and the OCA says “more than twenty years”. The oldest chronicle of his life, the *Historia Acephala*, gives the length of his exiles almost to the day. Robertson's dates add up to about seventeen and a half years.

cite.text: Gibbon, The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire, chapter 21; OCA; Robertson, Prolegomena (1892)

myths.claim: He spent six years hiding in a dry well.
myths.truth: That is Rufinus's tale, of a dry cistern. Robertson calls it “probably a confused version” of the plain fact that he hid in the monks' cells. Palladius says a young woman hid him in her house. No one knows for sure.

cite.text: Robertson, Prolegomena (1892); Palladius, Lausiac History, chapter 63

myths.claim: He escaped to Spain and hid as a cook in a monastery.
myths.truth: A later legend, kept in the *Acta Sanctorum*. Robertson mentions it with an exclamation mark. His exiles took him to Trier, to Rome and Italy, and into the Egyptian desert. He never went to Spain.

cite.text: Robertson, Prolegomena (1892)

circle.name: Antony the Great
circle.text: The father of the monks. Athanasius says he saw him many times, and “poured water on his hands”. Antony came to Alexandria to stand with him, and dying, left him a sheepskin and the cloak Athanasius had once given him new.

cite.text: Life of Antony, chapters 1, 69 to 71 and 91

circle.name: Basil the Great
circle.text: Bishop of Caesarea, who looked to him to heal the split among the Eastern churches. They wrote to each other, and Basil hoped one day to see him.

cite.text: Basil, Letters 66, 69, 80 and 82

circle.name: Gregory of Nazianzus
circle.text: Preached the great sermon on him at Constantinople, about seven years after his death.

cite.text: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 21

circle.name: Alexander of Alexandria
circle.text: His bishop. He brought him up for the Church, made him his deacon and secretary, and took him to Nicaea.

cite.text: Sozomen, Church History, Book 2, chapter 17

circle.name: Arius
circle.text: The Alexandrian priest who taught that the Son of God was created. Athanasius would not take him back. Arius died suddenly in Constantinople in 336, just before he was to be received back.

cite.text: To the Bishops of Egypt, chapters 18 and 19; Robertson's table

circle.name: Eusebius of Nicomedia
circle.text: The bishop who led the other side. Athanasius says he “buys the Meletians with large promises” to bring charges against him.

cite.text: Apology against the Arians, chapter 59

circle.name: Constantius II
circle.text: The emperor who drove him out twice, and sent troops for him in 356. Athanasius compared him to Antichrist.

cite.text: History of the Arians, chapter 76

circle.name: Julian
circle.text: The emperor who turned back to the old gods. He called Athanasius “that enemy of the gods”.

cite.text: Julian, Letter 46

circle.name: Arsenius of Hypsele
circle.text: The Meletian bishop he was said to have murdered. He turned up alive at Tyre, and later made his peace with Athanasius.

cite.text: Socrates, Church History, Book 1, chapter 29; Apology against the Arians, chapter 69

circle.name: Frumentius
circle.text: A young man who had helped run a kingdom beyond Egypt: India, Socrates calls it, and Ethiopia in the Coptic memory. He came to Alexandria asking for a bishop for the Christians there, and Athanasius made him that bishop. The Copts remember him as Abba Salama.

cite.text: Socrates, Church History, Book 1, chapter 19; Coptic synaxarium, 7 Pashons

circle.name: Julius of Rome
circle.text: The bishop of Rome who took him in, in 339, and whose council declared him innocent.

cite.text: Apology against the Arians, chapters 20 to 35

circle.name: Marcellinus
circle.text: The friend, ill and reading the Psalms, to whom he wrote the letter behind our Psalm quiz.

cite.text: Letter to Marcellinus

circle.name: George of Cappadocia
circle.text: The rival bishop Constantius put in his place in 357. A pagan mob killed him in 361.

cite.text: Gregory of Nazianzus, Oration 21, chapters 16 and 26; Robertson's table

death.big: He died at home in Alexandria on 2 May 373, bishop of his city, after seven quiet years. He was about seventy-five.
paras: After his last return, no emperor moved against him again. Socrates says Valens held back while he lived, because he knew that “the multitude of those who were attached to Athanasius was very great”.
In those years he built a new church, begun in 368 and finished in 370. He wrote to Basil in Cappadocia, who looked to him as the one bishop who could still bring the East together.

He named Peter, one of his clergy, to follow him. Socrates calls Peter “a devout and eloquent man”. Soon after, Valens let the Arians set up a bishop of their own, Lucius. Peter was jailed, escaped, and fled to Damasus, bishop of Rome.
Gregory of Nazianzus summed it up: “In a good old age he closed his life, and was gathered to his fathers, the Patriarchs, and Prophets, and Apostles, and Martyrs, who contended for the truth.”

later.title: Where his body went
later.text: Later accounts say his body was taken to Constantinople, “an event surrounded with no little uncertainty”, Robertson writes. Then to Venice, where, the story goes, a sea captain brought it after stealing it from a church in Constantinople. Robertson tells it drily: the body “decisively proved its identity by prodigies which left no room for doubt”.

cite.text: Robertson, Prolegomena (1892), after the Acta Sanctorum for 2 May

saint.big: Yes. Catholics, Orthodox, Copts, Anglicans and Lutherans all honour him.

churches.note: A Lesser Festival in the Church of England

paras: He was honoured soon after he died. Within about seven years Gregory of Nazianzus was preaching on his feast day in Constantinople.
No miracle is told of him. Robertson wrote: “Not a single miracle of any kind is related of him.” His name as a saint rested, he said, “on his life and character alone”.
The Roman calendar keeps him as a bishop and Doctor of the Church. The 1916 *Roman Martyrology* put it like this:

quotes.q: Although almost all the world had formed a conspiracy to persecute him, he courageously defended the Catholic faith…

cite.text: The Roman Martyrology (1916)
